title: KS3 Geography — Water Resources Reading
subtitle: Reading passages for water resources, scarcity, drought, management and UK water challenges.
description: Five KS3 reading passages with retrieval, inference and explanation questions. The passages are grounded in the water resources source material and cover physical processes, uneven access, drought, management choices and UK examples.

data.chapter: KS3 Geography Study Pack: Water Resources
data.sourceTitle: The Water Cycle As A System
data.targetTitle: The Water Cycle As A System
data.sourcePassage: The water cycle is powered mainly by the Sun and gravity. The Sun heats water in oceans, lakes, rivers, soil and vegetation, causing evaporation and transpiration. Water vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds before returning to Earth as precipitation. On land, water can be intercepted by vegetation, soak into soil as infiltration, move through soil as throughflow, move through rock as groundwater flow, or travel quickly over the surface as runoff. These flows connect stores such as rivers, lakes, aquifers, soil, ice, reservoirs and the atmosphere. A drainage basin is the area drained by a river and its tributaries, so actions upstream can affect people and ecosystems downstream.

questions.question: What two forces mainly power the water cycle?
questions.modelAnswer: The Sun and gravity.

questions.question: Which process changes liquid water into water vapour?
questions.modelAnswer: Evaporation

questions.question: Explain why the water cycle is better described as a system than as a simple circle.
questions.modelAnswer: It has many stores and flows, and water can move through different routes or remain stored for different lengths of time.

questions.question: How can an action upstream affect people downstream?
questions.modelAnswer: Pollution, dams or water abstraction upstream can change water quality or reduce the amount of water reaching downstream users.

questions.question: Which pair contains one store and one flow?
questions.modelAnswer: Reservoir and infiltration

data.chapter: KS3 Geography Study Pack: Water Resources
data.sourcePassage: Water access means whether people can get enough safe and affordable water for daily life. Access is uneven because both physical and human factors matter. Physical factors include rainfall amount, rainfall reliability, temperature, evaporation, geology, distance from rivers and seasonal drought. Human factors include poverty, sanitation, pollution control, conflict, governance, education, technology and the quality of pipes, pumps and treatment works. This means water scarcity does not only happen in dry places. A wet area can still have economic water scarcity if people cannot access clean water safely. A dry but wealthy coastal area may reduce shortages with reservoirs, efficient water use and desalination, although these options can be expensive and may affect the environment.

questions.question: Name one physical factor that affects water access.
questions.modelAnswer: Rainfall amount, rainfall reliability, temperature, evaporation, geology, distance from rivers or drought frequency.

questions.question: Name one human factor that affects access to clean water.
questions.modelAnswer: Poverty, sanitation, pollution control, conflict, governance, education, technology or infrastructure.

questions.question: Why might a wet place still have poor access to clean water?
questions.modelAnswer: It may have economic water scarcity if wells, pipes, sanitation or treatment systems are poor, or if pollution makes water unsafe.

questions.question: Which example best describes physical water scarcity?
options: A dry region has too little rainfall to meet demand
A wet village has polluted wells and no treatment
A city has broken pipes after conflict
questions.modelAnswer: A dry region has too little rainfall to meet demand

questions.question: Explain why desalination is not a perfect solution for water scarcity.
questions.modelAnswer: It can provide freshwater near coasts, but it is expensive, uses lots of energy and can create salty brine that may harm marine ecosystems.

data.chapter: KS3 Geography Study Pack: Water Resources
data.sourceTitle: Drought In The Horn Of Africa
data.targetTitle: Drought In The Horn Of Africa
data.sourcePassage: The Horn of Africa includes countries such as Somalia, Ethiopia, Kenya and Eritrea. Parts of the region have experienced severe droughts when seasonal rainfall has been unreliable or repeated rainy seasons have failed. High temperatures increase evaporation, so soils and water holes can dry out more quickly. Many people rely on rain-fed farming and livestock, which makes them vulnerable when rainfall is low. Poverty and conflict can make drought harder to manage because wells, roads, aid and water systems may be limited or damaged. Impacts can be social, economic and environmental: people may walk further for water, children may miss school, crops may fail, livestock may die, food prices may rise, vegetation may dry out and soil erosion may increase.

questions.question: Name one country in the Horn of Africa mentioned in the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: Somalia, Ethiopia, Kenya or Eritrea.

questions.question: Which livelihood is especially vulnerable to drought in this passage?
questions.modelAnswer: Rain-fed farming and livestock keeping

questions.question: Explain how high temperatures can make drought impacts worse.
questions.modelAnswer: High temperatures increase evaporation, so soils, water holes and vegetation dry out faster.

questions.question: Give one social and one economic impact of drought from the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: A social impact is people walking further for water or children missing school. An economic impact is crop failure, livestock deaths or rising food prices.

questions.question: Why can poverty and conflict make drought harder to manage?
questions.modelAnswer: They can limit or damage wells, roads, aid systems and water infrastructure, making it harder to supply safe water and support people.

data.chapter: KS3 Geography Study Pack: Water Resources
data.sourcePassage: Water management means planning how to supply, use, protect and conserve water. Good management usually combines several strategies. Dams and reservoirs can store water for dry periods and may generate hydropower, but they are expensive and can flood land or affect river ecosystems. Water transfer can move water from wetter areas to drier or more populated areas, but donor areas may object. Desalination can make freshwater from seawater, yet it needs large amounts of energy and produces salty brine. Demand can also be reduced by fixing leaks, using meters, educating people, reusing greywater, collecting rainwater and using drip irrigation on farms. The best option depends on cost, fairness, environmental impact and local water needs.

questions.question: What is water management?
questions.modelAnswer: Planning how to supply, use, protect and conserve water.

questions.question: Which strategy delivers water directly to plant roots?
questions.modelAnswer: Drip irrigation

questions.question: Explain one benefit and one limitation of dams and reservoirs.
questions.modelAnswer: They can store water for dry periods or generate hydropower, but they can be expensive, flood land and affect river ecosystems.

questions.question: Why is reducing demand often important before building a new supply scheme?
questions.modelAnswer: It can save water that is already available, reduce waste and may be cheaper or less damaging than building major new infrastructure.

questions.question: What factors should be considered when choosing the best water management strategy?
questions.modelAnswer: Cost, fairness, environmental impact, local water needs and whether the strategy reduces demand or improves supply safely.

data.chapter: KS3 Geography Study Pack: Water Resources
data.sourcePassage: The UK is often thought of as wet, but water resources are uneven. Western and northern areas are generally wetter because moist Atlantic air brings more rainfall, especially over upland areas. Eastern and south-eastern areas are generally drier, flatter and more densely populated. This creates a mismatch: some wetter areas have lower demand, while some drier areas have high demand. South-east England can face pressure because of population density, businesses, relatively low rainfall, dry summers, leaking old pipes and demand from homes and gardens. Impacts may include hosepipe bans, lower river levels, stress on chalk streams and debates about reservoirs, water transfers and metering. The UK can also experience flooding when heavy rainfall, saturated soils and urban surfaces send runoff quickly into rivers and drains.

questions.question: Which parts of the UK are generally wetter?
questions.modelAnswer: The west and north of the UK are generally wetter.

questions.question: Why are western and northern areas generally wetter?
options: Moist Atlantic air brings rainfall, especially over uplands
questions.modelAnswer: Moist Atlantic air brings rainfall, especially over uplands

questions.question: Explain why south-east England can face water stress.
questions.modelAnswer: It is relatively dry and densely populated, with high demand from homes, businesses and gardens, especially during dry summers.

questions.question: Give two possible impacts of water stress in south-east England.
questions.modelAnswer: Hosepipe bans, lower river levels, stress on chalk streams, higher management costs or debates about reservoirs and transfers.

questions.question: How can the UK experience both drought risk and flooding?
questions.modelAnswer: Dry periods can reduce reservoirs, rivers and aquifers, while intense rainfall on saturated ground or urban surfaces can increase runoff and flooding.
